1.q: אֲרוֹמִמְ⁠ךָ֣ אֱלוֹהַ֣⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ וַ⁠אֲבָרֲכָ֥ה שִׁ֝מְ⁠ךָ֗ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֥ם וָ⁠עֶֽד
1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [I will exalt you, my God, the King, yes, I will bless your name forever and ever]

David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who you are]

The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [continually]

2.note: David is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who you are]

The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for all time]

3.note: The expression **being much praised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is people. Alternate translation: [people praise him very much]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how great he is]

4.q: דּ֣וֹר לְ֭⁠דוֹר יְשַׁבַּ֣ח מַעֲשֶׂ֑י⁠ךָ וּ⁠גְב֖וּרֹתֶ֣י⁠ךָ יַגִּֽידוּ
4.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Generation to generation will proclaim your works; indeed, they will declare your mighty acts]

4.q: דּ֣וֹר לְ֭⁠דוֹר יְשַׁבַּ֣ח מַעֲשֶׂ֑י⁠ךָ וּ⁠גְב֖וּרֹתֶ֣י⁠ךָ יַגִּֽידוּ
4.note: The pronoun **your** refers to Yahweh. The pronoun **they** refers to the generations mentioned in the first part of the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Generation to generation will proclaim your works, Yahweh, and the generations will declare your mighty acts, Yahweh.]

5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **splendor**, **glory**, and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how splendidly glorious and majestic you are]

The terms **splendor**, **glory**, and **majesty** mean similar things. David is using these terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [your very great majesty]

6.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people and generations mentioned in 145:4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [generations of people will tell]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that you are great]

7.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [They will pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your goodness; indeed, they will sing joyfully about your righteousness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **remembrance**, **abundance**, **goodness**, and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [They will remember your abundant good ways, and they will sing joyfully, celebrating your righteous acts]

Here David is speaking as if speech about God’s goodness were a liquid that people **pour forth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will eagerly tell their]

8.note: David is using **long of nostrils** as a common expression of the culture to mean “slow to become angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [slow to anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithfully keeping his covenant]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his compassionate acts]

10.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [All your works will thank you, Yahweh; indeed, your faithful will bless you]

David is speaking of **all your works** as if they were living things that could **thank** God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everything you have made shows how good you are, Yahweh]

David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your faithful people]

11.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [They will tell the glory of your kingdom; yes, they will speak of your power]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory**, **kingdom**, and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how gloriously you rule, and they will speak of how powerful you are]

12.q: לְ⁠הוֹדִ֤יעַ ׀ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י הָ֭⁠אָדָם גְּבוּרֹתָ֑י⁠ו וּ֝⁠כְב֗וֹד הֲדַ֣ר מַלְכוּתֽ⁠וֹ
12.note: Here, **to make known** marks the following phrases as the goal or purpose of telling about God’s kingdom and power in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that the sons of man will know his mighty acts and the glory of the splendor of his kingdom]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to people everywhere]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory**, **splendor**, and **kingdom**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how gloriously and splendidly he rules]

The terms **glory** and **splendor** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the glorious splendor]

David has been addressing Yahweh directly in the second person, saying **your kingdom** and **your power** in the previous verse, but here he speaks of Yahweh in the third person, saying **his mighty acts** and **his kingdom**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person to be consistent. Alternate translation: [your mighty acts and the glory of the splendor of your kingdom]

13.q: מַֽלְכוּתְ⁠ךָ֗ מַלְכ֥וּת כָּל־עֹֽלָמִ֑ים וּ֝⁠מֶֽמְשֶׁלְתְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠כָל־דּ֥וֹר וָ⁠דֽוֹר
13.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Your kingdom is a kingdom of all of eternities; indeed, your dominion is in every generation and generation]

The psalmist is repeating the word **generation** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [succeeding generation]

13.q: מַֽלְכוּתְ⁠ךָ֗ מַלְכ֥וּת כָּל־עֹֽלָמִ֑ים וּ֝⁠מֶֽמְשֶׁלְתְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠כָל־דּ֥וֹר וָ⁠דֽוֹר
13.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **kingdom** and **dominion**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You rule as king over everything for all of eternities, and you reign supremely over every generation and generation]

14.note: Here David is speaking as if those of God’s people who are afflicted were **the ones being bowed down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones experiencing hardships]

15.note: Here, **the eyes of all** represents all creatures looking to God. David is using one part of the body to represent the whole creature’s action of waiting expectantly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All created beings]

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you are giving** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is Yahweh himself who provides food. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you yourself are giving]

16.note: David is using **opening your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “giving generously.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [giving generously]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with what they desire]

18.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [truthfully]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the ones fearing him desire]

The pronouns **their** and **them** refer to the ones who fear Yahweh, mentioned earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [he hears the cry of those who fear him, and he saves those who fear him]

20.note: David is drawing a contrast between how Yahweh treats those who love him and how he treats the wicked. Use a connector in your language that indicates this contrast. Alternate translation: [however, he destroys all of the wicked]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the wicked people]

21.note: Here, **my mouth** represents David himself in the act of speaking. David is using one part of the body to represent his whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I myself]

Here, **all flesh** represents all living people and creatures. David is using one aspect of the body to represent all living beings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all living creatures]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [him, the one who is holy,]

The terms **forever** and **ever** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for all time]

21.q: תְּהִלַּ֥ת יְהוָ֗ה יְֽדַבֶּ֫ר־פִּ֥⁠י וִ⁠יבָרֵ֣ךְ כָּל־בָּ֭שָׂר שֵׁ֥ם קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ
21.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **praise** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [My mouth will speak words that praise Yahweh, and all flesh will bless the name of the one who is holy]
